pages.title: The DOL starter
pages.for: Starting a cage motor straight on the full supply. Start pulls the contactor in. The latching contact keeps its coil fed. Anything that opens the coil circuit drops it out until Start is pressed again.
pages.rule:
Start (3) N/O, with the latching contact (7) across it.
Stop (8) N/C and the overload's contact (10) in series with the coil (4).
Extra Stops go in series, extra Starts in parallel with Start.
Coil voltage must match its wiring: 230 V phase to neutral, 400 V across two lines.

DOL start: usually 6 to 8 × full-load current, sometimes over 10.
Overload set to full-load current: holds at 1.05 ×, trips slowly at 1.2 × on its trip curve.
Star-delta: about a third of the current, about a quarter of the torque.

Runs only while Start is held: check 7. Will not start: check the overload first.

traps.text: The coil pulls and holds the main contacts. The latching contact only keeps the coil fed once Start springs back.
traps.cite: [^14] [^15] DOL study sheet; Basic Motor Control

traps.text: After a power cut the motor stays stopped until someone presses Start. That is no-volt protection.
The overload does not clear a short circuit. Fuses or a breaker do.
Set the overload to the motor's full-load current, not a trip current.
Isolate, lock off and prove dead first. A contactor can hold line voltage with its coil off.

pages.where: Pumps, fans and compressors. The supply, not the starter, sets how big a motor can start this way.

pages.name: How it works
pages.text:
Start (3), Stop (8) and the overload's contact (10) are in series with the coil (4). The [[latching contact]] (7) is wired across Start. The coil is fed phase to neutral, at 230 V.

When Start is pressed, the coil pulls the contactor in. The main contacts (5) close and the motor starts on the full supply. The latching contact closes too, so the coil stays fed through 7 when Start springs back.

Break that circuit anywhere and the coil lets go. It stays out until Start is pressed again.

pages.name: The starter, live
pages.text: When Start is pressed, the coil pulls in the main contacts and the latching contact together. On the example motor the meter jumps to about 162 A, then falls to 23.1 A as the motor runs up. When Start is let go, the coil stays fed through 7. Stop, the overload's contact 10, or a supply cut each open the coil circuit. The motor then stays stopped until Start is pressed again.

The motor runs and draws 23.1 A. At 100% of its setting the bar stays empty. Example values: the showroom motor, 23.08 A at full load, with the overload set to match.

Example values: the showroom motor, 23.08 A at full load, with the overload set to match. A start surge of 7 times for 4 s, and a 1 s supply cut. The overload runs on a sped-up clock. Only the motor current slider heats it, not the start surge.

pages.name: Check
pages.task: The motor is running. The supply fails for a second, then comes back. Nobody touches the buttons. What does the motor do?
pages.answer: It stays stopped until someone presses Start
pages.alt: L1 L2 L3 N 1 Fuses or breaker: short-circuit protection 2 8 Stop 3 Start 7 4 10 5 9 6 A Line current 1 Supply 6 Motor 2 Isolator 7 Latching contact 3 Start, N/O 8 Stop, N/C 4 Coil 9 Overload heaters 5 Main contacts 10 Overload contact Fed Not fed Moves as one Overload heat: 10 opens when it is full With no supply the coil let go, and 7 opened with the main contacts. When the supply returns, Start and 7 are both open, so the coil has no path. That is no-volt protection. A pump run by a float or pressure switch is different.
options: It stays stopped until someone presses Start
It starts again by itself when the supply returns
It keeps running, because the latching contact holds the contactor in
pages.html: With no supply the coil let go, and 7 opened with the main contacts. When the supply returns, Start and 7 are both open, so the coil has no path. That is no-volt protection. A pump run by a float or pressure switch is different. That switch stays made, so the pump restarts by itself when the supply returns.

pages.name: How it behaves
pages.text:
Starting current: The full supply goes on at once. It usually draws 6 to 8 times rated current, sometimes over 10 times. The supply voltage dips.

Starting torque: Full as well. Up to about 30 kW it is often 1.5 to 2.5 times rated. Check the data sheet.

The contactor: It makes the full starting current, but breaks only the running current.

Quick restarts: Restarting while it still turns can give up to twice the normal peak. Let it stop first.

pages.name: Where it is used
pages.text:
Used for: Pumps, fans and compressors. The simplest start: one contactor, an overload and two buttons.

Size: The supply sets the limit, because it must stand the voltage dip. Rules of thumb run from 4 to 5.5 kW. Sites with their own supply start motors up to 250 kW or more.

At sea: The generators are the supply. Large motors started one after another, like thrusters while manoeuvring, can dip the voltage badly.

Limit: It does nothing to cut the starting current. Where that is too much, use star-delta.

pages.name: Star-delta
pages.text:
Start in star, run in delta. In star each winding gets 400 ÷ √3 = 231 V, so √3 less current.

Each line also carries one winding's current, not √3 times it. So star draws 1 ÷ 3 of the DOL current and about a quarter of the torque.

It needs three contactors, a timer and a delta-run motor. Start it light. It peaks again at the switch.

Its overload sits on the main contactor, set to 0.58 × 23.08 = 13.4 A.

pages.name: Faults and tests
pages.text:
Safety first: Isolate, lock off and prove dead. A dropped-out contactor can still be live on its supply side.

Will not start: Check the overload (10) first, then Stop (8) and the coil (4).

Runs only while Start is held: Check the latching contact (7) and its wiring.

Overload trips: Check it is set to full-load current. It trips slowly at 1.2 times. Then look for a real overload, frequent starts or worn main contacts.

Short circuit: Fuses or a breaker clear it, not the overload.

pages.name: Coil faults
pages.text:
Chatters or buzzes: Look for low coil voltage, a loose connection or dirty magnet faces. As it pulls in, it should see 0.85 to 1.1 times its rating. Measure that live, then isolate again before you touch anything.

Wrong coil: Match its marked voltage to its wiring. A 230 V coil across two lines gets 400 ÷ 230 = 1.74 times its rating and can burn out. A 400 V coil from phase to neutral gets 230 ÷ 400 = 0.575 times. It may not pull in, and can overheat.

pages.name: Find the fault
pages.task: You press Start and the motor runs. You let go of Start and it stops. What is the likely cause?
pages.answer: The latching contact (7) is not making
pages.alt: L1 L2 L3 N 1 Fuses or breaker: short-circuit protection 2 8 Stop 3 Start 7 4 10 5 9 6 A Line current 1 Supply 6 Motor 2 Isolator 7 Latching contact 3 Start, N/O 8 Stop, N/C 4 Coil 9 Overload heaters 5 Main contacts 10 Overload contact Fed Not fed Moves as one Overload heat: 10 opens when it is full Start feeds the coil while you hold it. Once it springs back, only 7 can keep the coil fed, so 7 or its wiring is open.
options: The latching contact (7) is not making
The Stop button (8) is stuck open
